question:
I'm currently learning SQL Server 2008 and have come across schemas and there is one thing I don't understand about them that they have to have an owner; why can't they own themselves?

My background is mostly with Java and it sounds like a schema is like a package which does not have an owner.
answer_raw: Schemas are not namespaces like Java packages, they are security principals. In SQL Server every securable must be owned by a database principal, and ownership determines permission inheritance. When you create a schema you must specify an owner because the engine needs a principal to grant the schema itself permissions to, and to resolve who can alter/drop it. If a schema owned itself there would be no principal to authenticate against and permission checks would be circular. The owner is typically a user or role, not the schema. You can think of schema owner as the entity that implicitly has CONTROL on all objects in it and can transfer ownership. Changing owner moves the security boundary. This model lets you separate object namespace from permissions.

question:
A customer wants to rent a dedicated Server for their site. They do not need more than SQL Express 2017, for the time being, but they have been offered a dual Xeon system.

Does SQL Express install and work on a dual CPU system, albeit using just one CPU, or do they have to ask for a single CPU server?

Sorry but I haven't found an answer to this specific question.
answer_raw:
Yes, SQL Server Express 2017 will install and run on a dual-socket Xeon server. It does not require or refuse a single CPU. The edition's limit is one socket per instance, so on a dual CPU machine it will simply use one socket and ignore the other.

That means it will work, albeit you are paying for unused hardware. SQL Server Express 2017 is capped at one physical socket, up to four cores, and about 1.4 GB of buffer pool memory per instance, plus the 10 GB database size limit. The installer does not block dual CPU hosts; the engine will enumerate the hardware and self-limit to the Express caps.

If the server is dedicated to that one instance you will not gain anything from the second CPU. If you might later upgrade to Standard or run other workloads the dual Xeon is fine. Otherwise a single-socket system is cheaper and sufficient.

question: Is it safe to assume that ordering by an auto-incrementing PK in Postgres will order the records chronologically, from a creation standpoint? I have a many to many relationship, from which I don't need to track anything else except the relationship itself and some form of order of creation. I am trying to decide whether I need to incorporate a timestamp column for this, or whether I can reutilize the existing auto-incrementing PK column for that same purpose.

question:
Let's say for example there is an Ethernet switch, and there are four PCs connected to this switch. PC1 and PC2 are communicating with each other, and at the same time PC3 and PC4 are also communicating with each other. Obviously there is no Statistical TDM here. Also, there is only one node - the switch, so there cannot be multiple paths from source to destination.

So how does Ethernet become packet-switched? Is it because the data being exchanged are broken into packets? What are the conditions that must be satisfied to say that a network is a packet-switched network?
answer_raw:
Ethernet is packet-switched because the switch forwards independently addressed frames rather than reserving a continuous circuit. Each PC sends variable-length Ethernet frames with source and destination MAC addresses. The switch learns MACs, stores each complete frame in its buffer, then forwards it out only the port where the destination is known, allowing PC1-PC2 and PC3-PC4 traffic to interleave on the same physical medium without pre-allocation.

A network is packet-switched when data is divided into packets with headers containing destination information, packets are handled independently by store-and-forward nodes, and transmission is multiplexed statistically. The packets need not take the same path and need not be sent in fixed time slots. Circuit switching allocates dedicated bandwidth for the session; packet switching allocates resources per packet on demand. Breaking data into packets is necessary but not sufficient; the key is independent per-packet routing and buffering.

question:
Forgive me if this is a dumb question but I'm relatively new to the carrier networking world. We own a block of IP addresses, say a /18 and we advertise various /20s, /24s, /23s, etc all over the world. I want to know "what's available" from our space as in if there are portions that we are not advertising.

What I could do is download a text dump of the entire BGP routing table and grep for the /18, /19s, /20s, ... , /24s and see if there are any matches but there has to be a better way.

We use Juniper so I popped into a router and ran show route protocol bgp FIRST_IP_OF_18 but it only gave me a route to the first thing we advertise.
answer_raw:
You can see all advertised more-specifics inside your /18 with a single route lookup on a router that peers with the global table. Use show route 10.0.0.0/18 on inet.0, not show route protocol bgp FIRST_IP. That command returns the covering route and every longer prefix that is installed, so you get the /20, /23 and /24s you are actually originating and their next-hops.

For a global view, query a public BGP monitor for your origin ASN. RIS live, RouteViews or BGPStream will list every prefix the world sees from you. Export that list, sort it, and subtract from your allocated /18. Tools like bgpq3, ipcalc or a simple python set difference will show the holes.

If you only need what you are sending, use show route advertising-protocol bgp <peer> and filter on your /18. That shows exactly which more-specifics leave your network.

question: What might be difference between sslvpn and site-site vpn . Which one among two is secure and it's significance
answer_raw:
SSL VPN provides remote user access to corporate resources over the internet using SSL/TLS, typically on port 443, with a browser or lightweight client. It authenticates individual users and grants selective access to applications or file shares. Site-to-site VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between two networks, usually using IPsec at the router or firewall level, making the networks appear locally connected.

Security differs by scope. Site-to-site is generally more robust for inter-network traffic because encryption is enforced by hardened appliances, no user devices are involved, and the tunnel is always on. SSL VPN security depends on endpoint hygiene, client software, and user behavior, making it more exposed to phishing and malware.

Significance lies in use case: SSL VPN for remote workforce mobility, site-to-site for branch connectivity and data center integration.

My company has recently switched to an Agile way of working and as a part of it we've started using SCRUM. While I'm very comfortable with it and feel that this way is superior to a traditional one, some of my teammates don't share the same opinion. In fact they are very skeptical about "all that agile stuff", and don't take it seriously. As an example, one of the teammates is always late on the meetings, and doesn't really care about it. The management IMO tries not to notice this (maybe because it's new, and it takes time for the people to get used to it).

My question is, how to address this issue while not raising a conflict inside the team?
answer_raw: Focus on shared team outcomes rather than defending Agile. Bring the issue up in a retrospective as a team norm, not a personal criticism. Ask the team what they need for meetings to be useful, and invite everyone to co-create ground rules for punctuality and participation. Offer to help the person succeed, maybe checking if meeting times or format are a barrier. Ask the Scrum Master to facilitate the conversation so it stays systemic. Keep it curious and collaborative, and let the team own the agreement, which reduces defensiveness and avoids making it a conflict between you and them.

question:
In an ideal world it is preferrable to meet the deadline with less bugs. But from your experience which is more preferrable/acceptable:

Meet the deadline but has a number of bugs because developer rush into things

Less bugs but not quite meet the deadline because the developer is very rigorous in writing the code
answer_raw:
From experience less bugs but missing the deadline is more acceptable. Shipping on time with known bugs damages trust faster than a short delay. Users forgive a late, stable release; they do not forgive data loss, crashes, or security flaws that force hotfixes and erode confidence.

Rushing creates technical debt that compounds. A few bugs in release become support tickets, rollback risk, and rework that costs more time than the delay would have. Rigorous code means fewer production incidents, lower maintenance, and faster iteration later.

That said, the delay must be communicated early and bounded. Missed deadline without transparency is also damaging. Prefer a negotiated slip with clear quality gates over a deadline hit with compromised quality. In practice, delivering a reliable product slightly late preserves long-term velocity and reputation better than shipping broken on time.

question:
For a project I am working I want to implement a small prototype to try things out, demonstrate some functionality to the client and learn some frameworks used in the project.

Do you have any suggestions or do you know of best practices for implementing such a prototype?

Some more details:

The application will be a complex web app

I have to implement a mechanism where the server pushes data to subscribed clients (the data will be generated by some events)

I want to write a prototype which implements exactly this behaviour but nothing more
answer_raw: Keep the prototype minimal and isolated from the final architecture. Use a single event source, one server push channel, and one client subscription to prove the core flow. Choose the stack you will actually use, not a convenient mock, so learning transfers. For server push prefer WebSockets or Server-Sent Events over polling; SSE is simplest for one-way server-to-client events, WebSockets give full duplex if needed later. Use a lightweight in-memory broker like Redis Pub/Sub or an in-process channel to simulate events. Version the prototype and document the assumptions you are deliberately ignoring. Add a visible event log on both server and client for demo clarity. Time-box it to a day or two and define success as a reliable push from event to subscribed UI, nothing more.

question:
I understand the difference between the two, but I get questioned by my colleagues of the benefit of labeling requirements as functional or nonfunctional (or transitional). Why bother to do so? He spent what he said was two days going through a list of requirements for one project, and saw no benefit to it, because the end result was to submit the document to another business entity with the edict, "Do it all."

What I fear is requirements lumped together in one document. I tried to explain the benefit in practical terms, but couldn't sell it. How do I sell the benefit of documenting which requirements are functional and which are nonfunctional.
answer_raw:
Labeling isn't taxonomy for its own sake; it changes how the work is read and managed. Functional requirements define features and behavior, nonfunctional define quality attributes like performance, security, scalability, and transitional define migration and training. Different teams care about different sets, and they are verified differently.

With labels you can prioritize realistically, negotiate scope, and expose hidden cost. Nonfunctional requirements often drive architecture, technology choice, and budget, and they are the ones most often missed until production. You can also test and accept them differently.

When a customer says "do it all", the labels give you leverage to ask "all to what quality, by when, with what constraints?" It makes risk visible and prevents functional completeness with nonfunctional failure.

question: What tools / methodologies / strategies do you use to keep organized in doing your work as a developer? Can you provide details?
answer_raw:
I rely on a mix of lightweight process and tooling. For planning I use GitHub Projects with Kanban columns for backlog, in progress, review, done, paired with issues that have clear acceptance criteria. Daily work lives in a time-boxed TODO list in Obsidian, synced across devices, where I capture tasks from standups and split them into sub-tasks under 90 minutes.

Code is organized via trunk-based development with feature branches, conventional commits, and PR templates that enforce checklist, tests, and docs. Locally I use VS Code with dev containers for reproducible environments and pre-commit hooks for linting and formatting.

For context switching I keep a single source of truth for notes and ADRs, and do a 10 minute end-of-day shutdown ritual to update tickets, log blockers, and plan tomorrow’s top three.

question:
I have a very small and basic web site on a web server. Usually I'm doing the changes on a localhost where the development version is, and after that I upload it to the server with FileZilla. That's the very obvious way, but it's not the most convenient.

I've worked with SVN, but I've never needed to set anything - just checkout, commit, update. Reading some tutorials I wonder is this the easier way to upload the files to a server? Or are there any easier?
answer_raw:
SVN can work but Git is simpler now and gives you history on your laptop without needing a server-side setup for basic use. Keep a local Git repo, commit changes locally, then push to the live server with a single command or a post-receive hook that checks out to the web root. That removes manual FileZilla drag-and-drop and gives you rollback for free.

For a tiny site, even simpler is rsync over SSH: rsync -avz --delete ~/site/ user@host:/var/www/site syncs only changed files and is idempotent. Pair it with a shell alias or a git hook and you get one-step deploys.

If you must stay with SVN, keep a working copy locally and run svn update on the server in a cron or manually, but Git’s distributed model avoids server-side conflicts and works offline.

question:
MVC is pretty straightforward. There is a Model, a Controller and a View. When we create a website, it all come together as 'client sends REST keyword request to server -> the server matches the requested URL to the controller action -> which then calls the model(s) for data gathering/processing, gets the result -> and returns the result back to the client as a HTML page (view)'.

What if we are talking about a pure RESTful API web service? Then the flow with be something like 'client sends REST keyword request to server -> the server matches the requested URL to the controller action -> which then calls the model(s) for data gathering/processing, gets the result -> and returns the result back to the client in JSON'. Same as before, but there is no 'view'...or rather, the generated JSON can be thought of as a 'view'. In a sense, we are only utilizing the MC part of MVC. Is that how it is should be done? Or are there any other, better-suited patterns for a API-only service instead of MVC?
answer_raw:
For API-only services MVC still works, the View is just serialization. Most frameworks keep a thin Controller that handles HTTP concerns, delegates to an Application/Service layer, which orchestrates Domain/Model logic, then returns DTOs to be serialized to JSON. The Controller should not contain business logic.

This is essentially a layered or Clean Architecture variant. Common refinements are Resource-Based Controllers per aggregate, a separate Service/Application layer for use cases, and a Presentation layer for mapping to DTOs and validation. Hexagonal/Onion makes dependencies point inward to domain.

For read-heavy APIs CQRS separates commands from queries, and Repository pattern isolates persistence. The point is to keep HTTP, serialization and transport concerns out of the domain model, so the Model remains reusable and testable independent of REST.

question:
I migrated some files from one Version Control System to another. I have to prove that content are identical (between source and destination, denote 1 , 2). There are a few zips files (lets call them A B C) each of which contains hundreds of files. I am looking at best way to do CRC comparison between content in old VCS against the new one.

1) Generate CRC on each ZIP file as a whole and compare the CRC of 2 corresponding zips file. ZIP-ZIP CRC comparison.

Obviously, this approach will be easier. But I don't know what will include in calculation of CRC. Or even if CRC of two zip files with identical file content might be different.(modified date?).

2) Compare CRC of each files in zip against corresponding files. File-File CRC Comparison

with this approach, I will have to write a script that goes through each file in zip (say A1) and extract their CRC. Build a list with [path file name, crc]. do the same for zip(A2). Compare list.

Have anyone ever done something like this?
answer_raw:
Zip-to-zip CRC is unreliable. A ZIP stores per-file timestamps, compression flags, order and central-directory metadata, so two archives with identical payloads can have different bytes and CRC32. Even recompressing same content yields different archives.

Do file-to-file content hashing. Extract or stream each entry from both archives without fully unpacking, compute a strong hash like SHA-256 or BLAKE2 of the decompressed data, and compare by relative path.

With Python: zipfile.ZipFile(...).namelist(), read each info and hash(io.BytesIO(...)). Build dict path→hash for A1 and A2 and diff.

CRC32 is weak for proof; use cryptographic hash and keep a manifest. This proves content identity independent of archive metadata. Streaming avoids temp disk use. The manifest gives auditable proof that file contents match regardless of how the ZIP was created.

question: When considering what Windows event logs to incorporate into a SIEM solution, should I be looking at just the Security event logs, or all categories of event log? How useful are the other categories in detecting and responding to security incidents?
answer_raw:
Include far more than just Security. Security logs capture authentication, privilege use, object access and policy changes, and remain essential. But Application, System, DNS Client, PowerShell, Sysmon and the Microsoft-Windows-* operational logs provide context that makes those security events actionable.

System logs reveal service failures, driver loads, unexpected shutdowns and boot anomalies often preceding compromise. Application logs show malicious installers, Office macro execution and application crashes. PowerShell Operational and Module logs expose script-based attacks that may never generate a Security event. DNS Client and Web Proxy logs help map C2 communications.

For detection, correlation across logs reduces false positives and builds timelines. For response, non-security logs confirm impact, scope and persistence mechanisms. Collect them selectively to control volume but the broader Windows telemetry is what turns isolated Security alerts into investigable incidents.

question:
For a few years i stored my personal text files encrypted using an asymmetric key through GnuPG. Now i thought that it is a good idea to also encrypt my hard drive partition. Does it make sense to use both filesystem encryption (via, say, dm-crypt) and encryption via GPG for separate files? If this is unnecessary, what should i stick with for personal encryption of textual data?

I want to be able to use version control system and text processing tools on these files and also optionally apply steganography to conceal the existence of the files from intruders altogether.

I use GNU/Linux.
answer_raw: Use full-disk LUKS/dm-crypt for the partition and drop per-file GPG for day-to-day work. LUKS protects everything at rest, covers metadata and swap, and lets you edit files normally with git, editors and steganography tools without decrypt-encrypt cycles. GPG is useful for asymmetric sharing or archival of individual files, not for active editing. Storing plaintext under LUKS means steganography works on the real data, and git history stays readable while still confidential when the volume is locked. Double encryption adds complexity and key management burden with little benefit unless you need offline backups of especially sensitive files. question:
I'd like to know if Aescrypt is a valid tool, or if for a very secure protection, the only choice is to use a software like gpg, or similar.

More I've another curiosity, if one doesn't want to use encrypted email with a related software, could it be secure send AES encrypted files, through normal email connection ? Could it be usefull to use a rar AES protected archive, to further protect files ?

Thanks
answer_raw:
Aescrypt is a valid, open-source tool that implements AES-256 in CBC mode with a password-derived key. It is cryptographically sound for file encryption, though it lacks modern features like authenticated encryption, key exchange, or standardized passphrase hardening found in GPG.

GPG is not the only secure choice, but it adds asymmetric encryption, signatures, and a mature ecosystem. For very high security, GPG or age/minisign is preferable for key management and authenticity, not just confidentiality.

Sending AES-encrypted files by normal email is secure against transit eavesdropping, because the encryption protects content. Email itself is unencrypted in transit and stored in plaintext by providers, so metadata leaks and the risk of weak or shared passwords remain.

A RAR AES-protected archive can hide content, but RAR’s AES implementation is older and its password-based key derivation is weaker than modern tools. It also lacks authentication, so it is not more secure than Aescrypt and generally less auditable than GPG or age.

question:
For the purpose of a forensic mission, we must get a docker image without using the famous export from a docker command.

Does copy and paste of the folder /var/lib/docker/containers in another server allow us to retrieve information without any corrupted data?

Thanks.
answer_raw:
No. /var/lib/docker/containers holds only per-container metadata, JSON configs and logs, not the image layers themselves. Images live under /var/lib/docker/overlay2, aufs, btrfs, etc., and the image metadata is in /var/lib/docker/image/. Copying containers alone will not let you reconstruct an image and will give you incomplete forensic evidence.

Even copying the whole /var/lib/docker tree is risky without a proper preservation method. You need a consistent, read-only snapshot and archive with full metadata preserved: permissions, ownership, xattrs, extended attributes and timestamps. Use tar --xattrs --acls --same-owner --preserve-permissions or rsync -aHAX --numeric-ids. Avoid live copies; Docker writes constantly, so files can be torn and checksums will mismatch.

For forensics, image files should be acquired as a tar of the graph driver and image database, ideally from a quiesced host or snapshot, with hash verification.

question:
The use of paid API is increasingly rising each year. For example, IBM, Google and Microsoft are providing paid API such as Text to Speech, Speech to Text and Image to Text and vice versa.

I have a question about what happens If I build an app and publish it:

1.What happens when another person use Wireshack or reverse engineering to obtain the key of this API and then use it in their app or sell it?

2.Will I be paying for this even though my clients are not the people using this API?

3.Is there a way to reduce or prevent this from happening?

I am just worried about this and sure this is happening or must have happened at some point.

NOTE:

I asked this because I saw my Google Map API with the Wireshark software.

My initial solution is to make each user create username and password and apply restrictions to each individual user but those companies I mentioned up don't do that. They simply use one single key for their services.
answer_raw:
If someone extracts your API key with Wireshark and reverse engineering, they can make requests billed to your project. You are responsible for all usage tied to the key, not just your own users, so yes you will pay for their abuse until you stop it.

Providers mitigate this with key restrictions, not per-user logins. For Google Maps, restrict keys to specific Android app package name and SHA-1 fingerprint, iOS bundle ID, HTTP referrer for web, or IP ranges for servers. Rotate the compromised key immediately and create new ones per environment.

For sensitive APIs, proxy requests through your backend, keep the key server-side, authenticate your own users, and add rate limits and usage monitoring. This hides the key from clients and lets you revoke access per user without exposing credentials.

question: I know the difference between clustering and classification in machine learning, but I don't understand the difference between text classification and topic modeling for documents. Can I use topic modeling over documents to identify a topic? Can I use classification methods to classify the text inside these documents?
answer_raw:
Text classification assigns documents to predefined labels using supervised learning with labeled examples. The categories are known in advance, such as spam vs ham, news section, sentiment, and the model learns a mapping from text features to those labels.

Topic modeling is unsupervised. Models like LDA discover latent word co-occurrence patterns across a corpus and represent each document as a mixture of topics, without predefined names. Topics emerge from the data and must be interpreted afterward.

Yes, you can use topic modeling to identify topics in an unlabeled collection, giving exploratory insight. You can also use classification to label text inside documents, for example sentence-level sentiment or entity tagging, and classification requires labeled training data while topic modeling does not.

question:
Is it correct to say that any statistical learning algorithm (linear/logistic regression, SVM, neural network, random forest) can be implemented inside a Map Reduce framework? Or are there restrictions?

I guess there may be some algorithms that is not possible to parallelize?
answer_raw:
Not every statistical learner maps cleanly to MapReduce. MapReduce is batch, disk-based, and assumes independent mappers with a single shuffle-reduce, so iterative, sequential or stateful algorithms suffer.

Linear and logistic regression with gradient descent can be parallelized via data-parallel sums of gradients, and indeed are used in MapReduce with iterative MapReduce jobs. SVMs, especially kernel SVMs, need pairwise interactions and multiple passes, making them awkward and expensive; linear SVMs fare better.

Neural networks with backpropagation require many synchronized iterations and parameter servers; MapReduce’s high latency makes it impractical, though data-parallel SGD can be shoehorned with repeated jobs.

Random forests are embarrassingly parallel across trees, so they fit well.

Thus feasibility depends on iteration, communication and dependency, not just the model family.

question:
I was posting on stats.stackexchange but perhaps I should be posting here.

Context. Subscription business that charges users a monthly fee for access to the service. Management would like to predict "churn" - subscriptions who are likely to cancel. Management would like to create an email sequence in attempt to prevent high risk accounts from churning, perhaps with a discount code of some sort. So I need to identify those accounts at risk of leaving us.

I have a dataset with say 50k records. Each line item is an account number along with some variables. One of the variables is "Churned" with a value of "yes" (they cancelled) or "No" (they are active).

The dataset I have is all data since the beginning of time for the business. About 20k records are active paying customers and about 30k are those who used to be paying customers but who have since cancelled.

My task is to build a model to predict which of the 20k active customers are currently likely to churn.

Here is where I have tied my brain in a knott. I need to run the model (Predict) on the 20k records of active customers.

How do I split my data between training, test and predict?

Does predict data have to be exclusive of train and test data?

Can I split the entire dataset of 50k into 0.8 train and 0.2 test, build a model and then predict on the 20k active accounts? That would imply I'm training and testing on data that I'm also going to predict on. Seems "wrong". Is it?
answer_raw:
Yes, the accounts you will score must be completely excluded from training and testing. Training on the 20k currently active customers leaks their known No label into the model and gives optimistic performance. Those customers are the population you care about, so they should be a hold-out scoring set.

More importantly, churn is time dependent. Build a proper prediction task with a horizon, e.g. will churn in next 90 days. Create a training set from historical accounts with features as of a past date and outcomes observed after that date, and a test set from a later historical period. Only after validation, fit the final model on all usable history and score the current 20k actives, which were never used in training or testing.

question: As I was checking the /etc/fstab I noticed that the swap space has attr pass=0, which means its filesystem is not checked at boot time. Can anyone please tell me why is this behavior for?
answer_raw: Swap has no filesystem at all, so there is nothing for fsck to check. The pass field controls the order in which filesystems are scanned by fsck at boot, with 1 for root and 2 for others, and 0 to skip. Since swap is a raw device used for paging and hibernation, not a formatted filesystem, running a filesystem check makes no sense and would fail. The kernel activates swap with swapon, which only verifies the swap signature and size, not file structures. Setting pass to 0 explicitly tells the boot scripts to ignore the entry for fsck. The dump field is also normally 0 for swap. This is the standard and expected configuration on all Linux systems.

question: When we do k-fold cross validation, should we just use the classifier that has the highest test accuracy? What is generally the best approach in getting a classifier from cross validation?
answer_raw:
Cross-validation is for estimating generalization error and selecting hyper-parameters, not for picking a single fold’s model. The test accuracy in each fold is a noisy estimate; choosing the model from the fold with the highest score will overfit to that particular split and ignores the variance across folds.

The usual practice is to average the performance metrics across the K folds to obtain a stable estimate of error for a given configuration, and to select the hyper-parameters with the best mean score, often with a tie-breaker on lower variance. Once a configuration is chosen, the final classifier should be re-trained on the entire training set, not on a single fold, because using all data reduces variance and yields a model that is as representative as possible. If an unbiased estimate of test performance is needed, keep a held-out validation set separate from the CV loop.

question:
Say you're building a sales prediction model to predict tomorrow's sales value, as well as the next 2 weeks of daily sales. The model is being trained using daily data for the previous 1.5 years, and it follows a strong weekly seasonality pattern.

Obviously once you are happy with model performance, would it be necessary to re-train the model everyday to capture data up to and including yesterday in order to get the most accurate prediction for tomorrow's sales value? Essentially, the model would be trained on a rolling 1.5 year data set to capture yesterday's sales value.

Or does it depend on the type of model being used? Whether you need to to completely re-train when new data is present

I can see why it would make sense to re-train your standard time series forecasting models (ARIMA etc.), but I can also understand more sophisticated models (Neural Networks etc.) may generalize well enough to not have to re-train everyday.

I am looking for an explanation of models where you would and wouldn't re-train when new time series data is present.
answer_raw:
Yes, you generally want the model to see yesterday. For classic statistical models you almost always re-fit. ARIMA, ETS, and linear regression with lag features estimate parameters from the whole window; a new observation changes means, variances and autocorrelation, so the forecast for tomorrow shifts. Retraining daily on a rolling 1.5-year window is standard.

With state-space and exponential smoothing methods you can update recursively without a full refit, and with online learning algorithms you can incrementally adjust weights.

Deep neural nets can generalize and are less sensitive to one new day, but they still drift with promotions, seasonality shifts, and changing demand. Full daily retraining is often overkill; weekly or monthly retraining with a rolling window, plus continuous monitoring, usually gives the best accuracy-cost trade-off.

question: I'm looking for some common problems in unix system administration and ways that shell scripting can solve them. Completely for self-educational purposes. Also I'd like to know how would you go about learning shell scripting.
answer_raw:
Common sysadmin pain points are repetitive checks and cleanup. Shell scripts automate log rotation and archival with find + gzip, monitor disk usage with df and mail alerts when thresholds are exceeded, prune old user home directories, generate daily reports from journalctl or /var/log, and restart failed services via systemctl status checks. Scripts can also enforce backups with rsync and verify checksums.

Learn by reading man pages for core utilities, then practice small tasks: list top processes, parse /etc/passwd, loop over files. Build a personal cheat sheet, use shellcheck for errors, and automate one real daily chore. Re-read POSIX spec examples and modify them. Work in a VM or container, keep scripts in version control, and review them weekly to reinforce concepts.

question:
When i installed ubuntu in my x86 machine, I had to configure some memory as 'swap area'.

What is the use of this memory and what is the importance of this memory in linux file systems?

How can I determine the exact size of 'swap area' in a machine for the safe working of linux inside in it?
answer_raw:
Swap is virtual memory backed by disk that extends RAM. When physical memory fills, the kernel moves inactive pages to swap area to free RAM for active processes, preventing out-of-memory kills. It also allows hibernation, where RAM contents are written to swap.

In Linux filesystems swap is not a filesystem; it is a raw partition or file with swap signature managed by swapon. It is important for stability, memory pressure handling, and overcommit.

Size rule of thumb: for modern desktops with 8-16 GB RAM, 1-4 GB swap is enough; for servers, 1x RAM up to 32 GB. For hibernation, swap >= RAM.

Check current swap with `swapon --show`, `free -h`, or `cat /proc/swaps`. Plan size via `free -h` RAM and workload.

question: I am changing my current partition scheme (personal development laptop, dual boot) to remove the Windows partition and leave only my Slackware64 instance. What thought should go into my partitioning? I have been keeping / and /home in separate partitions, as well as a swap partition too. How do I decide what other partitions would be good to have in their own section of the disk?
answer_raw:
With one OS on a laptop, keep it simple and let the filesystem do its work. / and /home separate is sensible: / stays small and can be reinstalled without touching data, /home holds configs and projects. Swap is fine, but on modern RAM-rich laptops a small swap file is often enough.

Add partitions only for a clear operational reason. A small /boot on EFI systems, typically 512 MiB FAT32, is useful for firmware access. A separate /var can protect the root from log growth and make backups easier. /tmp can be tmpfs in Slackware to avoid disk wear. /srv or /opt only if you want strict quotas or different mount options.

Avoid over-partitioning: it makes resizing hard and wastes space. Use LVM or btrfs subvolumes for flexibility instead of many fixed partitions, and size /home generously for the remaining disk.

question:
How can I find out who executed a particular command and which terminal was used to run it?

Original:

How can I know particular cmd is executed by whom and to know about my terminal
answer_raw:
Use Linux audit subsystem to reliably track executions. Install and enable auditd, then add a rule like auditctl -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/target -k cmd_track. Later search with ausearch -k cmd_track -i or ausearch -c commandname. Output shows UID, user name, PID, PPID, tty and timestamp.

For recent interactive sessions, who, w and who -a list logged-in users and their tty or pts device. The kernel records the controlling terminal in /proc/PID/cmdline and /proc/PID/status. Environment variables TERM, SSH_CLIENT and SSH_CONNECTION reveal terminal type and remote source for ssh sessions. Bash history includes timestamped commands per user in ~/.bash_history, but it can be edited.

For persistent forensics combine audit logs with auth.log and journalctl -u sshd to correlate user login time with command execution.

question: Why are tables built into ipchains? What was the benefit of adding tables to ipchains? Is there a simple scenario that would illustrate how tables are used to increase performance or offer some other benefit?
answer_raw:
Ipchains started with a single flat rule set for input output forward. Tables split that work by function and by hook point so packets follow a defined pipeline instead of one monolithic list.

Each table owns its built in chains and is evaluated at a specific stage, which avoids mixing unrelated work, lets rules be loaded atomically per table, and allows fast short circuiting when a table decides the packet fate.

For a home router needing NAT and filtering, a single chain must test every filter rule for packets that only need translation and vice versa. With tables NAT runs first in prerouting, rewrites addresses once, then filter sees post NAT addresses.

A drop ssh rule lives in filter INPUT after translation while port forwards live in nat PREROUTING. Policy is clearer, duplicate checks disappear, and the common case is handled by the smallest relevant rule set.

question:
I am confused by the dual concepts of time-resolution and bandwidth. Often I will hear that a pulse-compressed radar application 'doesnt have enough BW' for some specific time resolution that is sought.

Isnt the maximum time resolution simply the reciprocal of your sampling rate?

How are those concepts related?
answer_raw:
Time resolution in radar is range resolution, not sample interval. A target’s echo must be distinguishable from a neighboring echo in time, which is set by the width of the compressed pulse.

For a simple uncompressed pulse, resolution ≈ pulse width. Pulse compression keeps energy long but yields an effective width ≈ 1/B where B is signal bandwidth. Range resolution is c/(2B). More bandwidth means a shorter autocorrelation main lobe and better ability to separate two returns.

Sampling rate sets the Nyquist limit and the time grid you can observe, fs must be ≥ 2B to capture the waveform without aliasing, so sample interval 1/fs is the quantization step, not the resolving power. You can sample fast with narrow bandwidth and still have poor resolution, or sample just enough for B and get the full 1/B resolution.

question: Can anyone state the difference between frequency response and impulse response in simple English?
answer_raw:
Impulse response shows how a system reacts over time to a sudden, very short kick. If you hit a bell, the impulse response is the ringing sound that follows, with its decay and resonances. It lives in time.

Frequency response shows how the system treats steady tones of different pitches. It tells you which frequencies are boosted, which are cut, and whether each tone is delayed. It lives in frequency.

One is the time-domain picture, the other is the frequency-domain picture. They contain the same information, linked by the Fourier transform. Knowing the impulse response lets you compute the frequency response, and vice versa. In practice engineers use impulse response for transients and frequency response for tone balance and filter design.

question:
I need help understanding how/what does it mean to "turn" a transformation parameters into a vote. I know how to recover the transformation parameters (in my case: 6 DOF), but how this turns into a vote in 6D (??) space ?

Thank You !
answer_raw: A vote is an accumulator cell in parameter space that a local measurement increments. For 6 DOF rigid pose you have e.g. tx,ty,tz,rx,ry,rz. Each correspondence or feature match gives a hypothesis for those six numbers. Instead of trusting it you increment the 6D histogram bin around that hypothesis, adding weight or confidence. Many independent local votes from different points accumulate. The true transformation receives many consistent votes from all inliers, forming a peak in the 6D accumulator. Outliers vote randomly and diffuse. Turning parameters into a vote means mapping the estimated tx,ty,tz,rx,ry,rz to an index in the 6D grid and adding +1 or a confidence weight there. Discretization makes the space sparse, and peak detection then recovers the consensus pose.

question:
I performed 512 point FFT on a signal. I got another set of 512 Numbers. I understand that those numbers represent amplitude of the various sine and cosine waves having different frequencies.

If my understanding is correct can somebody tell me how to know the frequencies of those sine and cosine waves from the knowledge of those 512-numbers (i.e amplitudes) ?
answer_raw:
The 512 FFT values are complex coefficients for discrete frequencies spaced by Fs/512. With sampling rate Fs and N=512, bin k corresponds to f_k = k·Fs/N for k=0…511. Bin 0 is DC, bin 1 is Fs/512, bin 2 is 2·Fs/512, etc. Up to Nyquist.

For real input the spectrum is conjugate symmetric, so bins 1 to 255 contain the unique positive frequencies, bin 256 is Nyquist if N even, and bins 257 to 511 mirror them. Magnitude |X[k]| gives amplitude, phase gives sine/cosine mix.

Thus frequency of bin k is k·Fs/512 Hz. If you know Fs, map each magnitude to its frequency. If Fs is unknown you can only give normalized frequency k/N cycles per sample.

question:
I have convolved a random signal with a a Gaussian and added noise (Poisson noise in this case) to generate a noisy signal. Now I would like to deconvolve this noisy signal to extract the original signal using the same Gaussian.

The problem is that I need a code which does the job of deconvolution in 1D. (I have already found some in 2D but my main aim is 1D).

Can you please suggest me some packages or programs that are able to do so? (Preferably in MATLAB)

Thanks in advance for the help.
answer_raw:
MATLAB’s Signal Processing and Image Processing Toolboxes already provide 1-D deconvolution. For Gaussian blur with Poisson noise use Richardson-Lucy, implemented as deconvlucy, which is maximum-likelihood for Poisson statistics and works on vectors by reshaping to column. deconvlucy(y, psf, numiter, options) returns the estimate.

For Gaussian noise use Wiener filtering: deconvwnr or wiener2 with 1-D input, or manual frequency-domain division Y./H with Tikhonov regularization to avoid division by zero: Xhat = ifft( Y.*conj(H) ./ (|H|^2 + lambda) ).

The Regularization Tools package offers deconvreg for Tikhonov/Total Variation regularization in 1-D. Alternatively implement Wiener in fft: H = fft(psf, N); Y = fft(y,N); Xhat = ifft( Y.*conj(H)./(abs(H).^2 + eps) ).

All methods need zero-padding and proper PSF centering.

question: I know the basic working principle of sinusoidal oscillators. But I have a doubt on this matter when I came across Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure. I have read that the source for sinusoid signal output from an oscillator is the noise. Due to controlled positive feedback a single frequency component is selected and amplified, right? If the noise is a white noise, we say it has all frequency components. We think in terms of all possible sinusoids with different frequencies. When coming to frequency response too, we think in terms of sinusoids. Why can't we think in terms of other orthogonal basis set? Although it makes life difficult, I would like to know the justification for thinking in terms of sinusoids. Is sinusoids the nature's default signals?
answer_raw: Sinusoids are not arbitrary; they are eigenfunctions of linear time-invariant systems. A constant-coefficient differential equation commutes with time shifts, so e^{jωt} is mapped to a scaled version of itself. Any other complete orthogonal set will be mixed by the system, making analysis hard. Noise is stationary, its autocorrelation depends only on delay, so by Wiener-Khinchin its representation diagonalizes in frequency. An oscillator is a resonant LTI feedback loop with poles near the imaginary axis; it selectively amplifies the eigenmode at that frequency present in the broadband noise. You can expand signals in wavelets, prolate spheroids, etc., and Gram-Schmidt will give an orthogonal basis, but the system response couples those basis elements. Sinusoids are nature's default for linear, time-invariant, passive media because Maxwell's equations and mechanical wave equations are translation invariant in time.

question: What's the correct way. Should I zero-pad a signal before or after applying a windowing function?
answer_raw: Window first, then zero-pad. The window is a time-domain operation intended to taper the actual data you have, suppressing spectral leakage at the segment edges. Apply it to the finite record you want to analyze, with the window length equal to the data length. Zero padding is a frequency-domain interpolation trick, not a way to create data. It is performed after windowing by appending zeros to the windowed sequence before the FFT, increasing FFT size for finer bin spacing without changing the underlying spectrum. Padding before windowing would let the window taper into the zeros, effectively modifying the window shape and the data's energy, and it changes the main-lobe width and sidelobe levels you intended. Keep windowing and zero padding separate: window the real data, then pad for interpolation.

question:
When energy is referred to as the square summable sequence, is that energy a representation of the power of the signal? How is the energy of frequency determined?

E.g. what if an audio signal has high energy on the higher frequencies and another has high energy on the lower, bass, frequencies, how is this determined?

What exactly is the power from the square summable series representing then and is it useful for audio?
answer_raw:
Energy of a discrete signal is sum of squared samples, sum |x[n]|², which is finite iff square-summable. That is total energy, not instantaneous power. Average power is energy divided by number of samples, or limit of energy per duration for infinite signals.

Frequency energy follows Parseval. The DFT magnitude squared gives energy per bin, up to 1/N scaling. Summing |X[k]|² equals N sum |x[n]|². So high bass vs treble is seen by which bins contain larger squared magnitudes.

The square-summable power is therefore a time-domain energy measure. In audio it is useful for loudness estimation, normalization, dynamic range control and spectral analysis, though perceived loudness also depends on frequency weighting. It maps to power spectral density for stationary signals.

question: What's the difference between these? Both are measurements of some form of signal power, but surely there's some difference between the power they are measuring?
answer_raw:
dBm is an absolute power level referenced to 1 milliwatt, normally into a 50 Ω system. dBmV is an absolute voltage level referenced to 1 millivolt at the terminals, not power per se.

You can only convert between them if you assume an impedance, typically 50 Ω or 75 Ω for RF/cable work. With a standard 50 Ω load, P = V²/R, so 0 dBmV = 1 mV rms ≈ 0.02 µW ≈ -47 dBm.

So the numbers look comparable but they describe different physical quantities. dBm tells you how much RF power is actually being delivered or received. dBmV tells you the voltage you would measure at a point, which is the convention in TV, CATV and baseband systems where receivers are voltage driven and the system impedance is fixed.

In practice dBm is used where power transfer and link budget matter, and dBmV is used where the signal is characterized as a terminal voltage. The difference is power vs voltage, and the implicit assumption about impedance that lets you go from one to the other.

question:
My understanding of Pulse Doppler Radar is the system measures Time Of Flight for the pulse.

My confusion is that during the down conversion process prior to ADC the lowpass filter causes some time delay in addition to the time of flight. In principle the delay should be known beforehand but I'm sure it's not exact and in general the delay is not completely constant even among the band of interest.

How is this delay dealt with?
answer_raw:
Pulse Doppler radars normally measure range by the arrival time of a pulse relative to transmit, and Doppler by the phase progression between pulses. The group delay introduced by the mixer, low-pass filter and ADC anti-alias chain is essentially the same for every pulse and is common-mode.

That constant delay therefore cancels in a differential measurement. For Doppler the absolute time offset produces a fixed phase offset that is removed when the phase difference from pulse to pulse is formed. For range the absolute offset is calibrated out once, e.g. by a loopback or a target at known range, and tracked as a system bias.

Modern systems design the baseband chain for linear phase so the group delay is flat over the signal bandwidth, making the residual variation negligible compared to the range resolution set by pulse width or bandwidth. Any remaining variation is compensated in digital matched filtering and timing alignment.

I want to construct a reference locked sine oscillator. The multibit sine wave is calculated using DDS. The multibit reference signal is typically not sinusoidal, can have offset and substantial noise, but is expected to contain one dominant frequency.

If this dominant frequency is nearly known, a standard PLL approach will work to keep track of the dominant frequency in the reference signal.

However, I now suppose this cannot work to acquire initial reference lock if the dominant frequency is far away from the oscillator frequency. In this case, the PLL gets stuck on a locally dominant frequency.

What is the common approach to resolve this ? Calculating an DFT seems like overkill, since it produces a lot of unnecessary information. A recursive 4 sample Zoom FFT looks a bit more efficient. But maybe there is a way that directly modifies the PLL filter to capture further off frequencies ?

Please let me know if I missed crucial info.

Run the DDS with a wideband frequency discriminator or a fast sweeping/gear-shifted PLL, then hand over to the normal PLL once the error is small. A practical implementation is a frequency-locked loop with a large loop bandwidth or a bang-bang/phase-frequency detector for acquisition, or a swept VCO/gear-change where you start with a wide capture range and progressively narrow it. Many designs simply measure the dominant tone once with a low-cost estimator – zero-crossing interval, autocorrelation peak, or a single-bin Goertzel/Zoom FFT tuned to the expected band – then pre-load the DDS and engage the PLL in track mode. That avoids a full DFT while still giving a reliable start frequency.
